summary:
Same-sex conduct between adults is legal in Madagascar, but only from age 21. Penal Code Article 331 treats same-sex acts involving a person under 21 as indecent assault, carrying five to ten years' imprisonment, so the age of consent is unequal and a visitor whose partner or counterparty is under 21 faces a serious criminal exposure that a heterosexual visitor does not.

Status on arrival is thin. There is no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions, no anti-discrimination law, and no legal gender recognition, so a trans traveller holds no locally recognised identity, no partner status and no named protection under Malagasy law.

Marriage is closed to same-sex couples. Article 2 of Law No. 2007-022 on Marriage and Matrimonial Regimes prohibits marriage between two persons of the same sex whether before the Civil Registrar or under traditional ceremonies. Article 39 of the same law names "gender identity" as a cause for absolute nullity of marriage, a direct legal exposure for trans people.

The social environment is the dominant practical factor. Homosexuality is not illegal, yet it is widely considered socially unacceptable, and LGBT Malagasy people conceal their lives in order to keep jobs and live in peace, relying on private networks and coded language (France 24, August 2024). Public expression is constrained: in early July 2021 the Malagasy government cancelled an LGBTQ party held at a bar in Antananarivo on the grounds of "incitement to debauchery".

Violence risk is documented and trans-specific. The U.S. State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report recorded general societal discrimination, with public attitudes ranging from tacit acceptance to violent rejection, particularly of transgender sex workers, who were frequent targets of verbal abuse, stone throwing and even murder. Supporters of a same-sex couple were subjected to insults and death threats on social media, and religious leaders publicly accused them of "promising homosexuality".

Official posture is hostile to protection measures. In Madagascar's fourth Universal Periodic Review (January 2025, 235 recommendations) the government rejected UN recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent. Six Malagasy organisations (Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers' Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage, Madagascar LGBT+) protested that "Refusing to act is to endorse impunity and condone violence."

Family and custody rights are restricted to heterosexual married couples: Article 33 of Law No. 2005-014 on Adoption states that "Full adoption is only permitted to heterosexual spouses." In a 2020 case, a 33-year-old woman was arrested for the statutory rape of a 19-year-old woman after the younger woman's mother filed a complaint, with the mother allegedly acting to cover up an incest and rape accusation against the father; religious leaders offered the young woman conversion therapy.

Access to care and health protection is addressed mainly through HIV policy. Act No. 2005-040 on the Fight against HIV/AIDS requires information, education and communication programs adapted to the sexual orientation of target groups, and Article 26 mandates special provisions to protect vulnerable groups, expressly including young people, sex workers, men who have sex with men and mobile populations, against HIV transmission.
tangentialFactors:
Madagascar sits within a regional pattern of partial decriminalisation: as of July 2020, roughly 22 of 53 African states had moved to decriminalise same-sex conduct, with Madagascar's decriminalisation qualified by the elevated age of consent.

Data-protection law offers a limited shield. Law No. 2014-038 on the Protection of Personal Data, Article 18, bars processing of sensitive data including data on health or sexual life, and Law No. 2017-045 on Credit Information Bureaus, Article 2, likewise protects sexual orientation as sensitive data.

The 2011 human rights reporting covered a post-coup period with unlawful killings and broader societal discrimination against women, persons with disabilities and the LGBT community, indicating weak state-protection capacity during political instability.
localsOnly:
Residents face a legal framework that is limited in progress compared with other countries: same-sex activity is legal for over-21s but LGBT Malagasy people lack civic rights such as marriage and adoption, and most civic liberties including the rights to marry and adopt children are not afforded to LGBTQ individuals.

Article 39 of Law No. 2007-022 names gender identity as a cause for absolute nullity of marriage, creating a standing legal vulnerability for trans Malagasy people entering marriages.

Community organisations including Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers' Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage and Madagascar LGBT+ operate domestically and publicly contested the government's UPR positions in January 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether any legal gender recognition procedure exists for trans Malagasy people beyond the marriage-nullity provision; no source addresses administrative marker change.

Whether the Penal Code's two-to-five-year penalty band for "indecent or against nature" acts applies to under-21s in parallel with Article 331's five-to-ten-year indecent-assault band is stated inconsistently across sources and remains unresolved here.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa screening that could disclose gender identity or HIV status at the border; that question is not sourced.

Enforcement frequency of Article 331 against adults and the practical availability of remedies after the 2021 party cancellation are not documented in the inventory.
